cells.tense: You are holding the whole spread of what this could feel like and still pointing at one door.
cells.ask: Take one option you have been weighing and put it on paper as the one you are taking, then start on the first small piece today.
cells.core:
The feelings that come with the choice are all in the room at once, and you are not drowning in them. You can sit with the whole range of what this might feel like and still point at one door and walk through it. Most people either shut the feelings out or get swept by them. You are keeping both in view, and the pick stays yours.

What's worth keeping: you can see the patterns in what you want and still let the want stay real, instead of flattening one into the other. Feeding this looks like taking one weighed option and setting it down as the one you are taking. Once it is written and started, new possibilities tend to show themselves to someone already moving. The cost is living with a real pick instead of keeping the door open.
cells.sheetLine: You gather every feeling at once and still choose.
cells.verb: gathering every feeling the choice might bring, all of it pulled in at once
cells.place: the chair where direction gets chosen — this, not that

cells.tense: You are gathering every feeling this could bring before anything has actually been decided.
cells.ask: Before the next round of imagining how each path will feel, write down one outcome you would accept, as a limit you are done negotiating with.
cells.core:
You want the one option that will feel right in every direction at once, so you keep gathering the feelings of all of them — the one that lands well, the one that keeps the door open, the one where nothing is lost. None of the imagining settles anything, because each new version brings an emotion you had not accounted for, and the gathering starts again.

The fix runs the other way: from all that reach an actual limit. Decide one thing that will hold even if the feelings shift — an end, a price, a thing you are not giving up. That is not the same as shutting down; it is what lets you choose without having felt everything first. Put the one you would accept where you can see it, and let it stay settled while the feelings move around it.

cells.tense: You let the decision go by while you were still gathering how it would feel.
cells.ask: Let the mind be still for ten minutes without deciding anything, then name one direction that has closed and set it down for good.
cells.core:
A decision went by while you were still feeling out how each option would go, and you have not been pointing at anything since. Not because the possibilities went away — they did not — but because the deciding itself stopped, and you got used to the pause. The pull of what might be felt is still there; the hand that picks between them is not in the room.

The way back is small and sideways. Stop the sheer trying for a minute — ten quiet ones, nothing to pick, nothing to feel. When the mind is still, you can see what got settled without you, and you can name one direction that closed and let it be closed. That clears enough room to point at a direction again.

cells.tense: You are steering by what each choice might feel like and calling it simply being open.
cells.ask: Go back and pick out one direction you have already moved on without saying so, and say out loud that you chose it.
cells.core:
You are already choosing. The direction has been bending for a while, and the way you linger on one possible feeling or reach for one path over another is the pick being made. You are doing it, and you describe yourself as just waiting for clarity while the options sit there.

But the pick is already on the record, made quietly, and naming it will not cost you anything except the story that you have not decided. Think of the last choice you moved on without announcing it — maybe a plan you started, maybe one you let go. Write it down and say you took that direction. That puts the decision back in your hands instead of leaving it as something that happened to you.

attempts.check: The record does not say the person has felt let down by what they chose before, so Too Little cannot claim that room or what it taught; I state only that the door closed and the deciding stopped, which the person can contradict and still use. Too Much crosses Compassion as gathering many possible feelings, not as saving the feeling for someone specific — the push is on hoped-for outcomes, not on a person; if my read is off, the ask still gives them a piece of the decision they can hold this week. The sentence that serves me more than them is anything implying they are afraid to choose; the floor is the deciding itself, not the fear.
